rows.stem: Oxidation of chloroform by air in the presence of sunlight produces a poisonous gas known as :
rows.solution:
Chloroform left in a part-empty bottle is slowly oxidised by atmospheric oxygen in sunlight to carbonyl chloride, \(\mathrm{COCl_2}\), which is better known as phosgene and is extremely poisonous:
\(2\mathrm{CHCl_3} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2\mathrm{COCl_2} + 2\mathrm{HCl}\)
This is why chloroform is kept in dark coloured bottles filled to the brim: the dark glass excludes the light and a full bottle excludes the air. Mustard gas and tear gas are unrelated compounds, and chlorine is not what forms here.

rows.stem: Lucas reagent produces cloudiness immediately with :
rows.solution:
Lucas reagent is concentrated hydrochloric acid with anhydrous zinc chloride, and the cloudiness is the insoluble alkyl chloride separating out. The reaction goes through a carbocation, so the speed follows carbocation stability. A tertiary alcohol gives a tertiary carbocation at once and turns the mixture cloudy immediately; a secondary alcohol takes about five minutes; a primary alcohol gives no cloudiness at room temperature at all.

Of the four, 2-methyl-2-propanol is the tertiary alcohol, so it is the one that reacts immediately. Butan-2-ol is secondary, and both 2-methyl-1-propanol and butan-1-ol are primary.

rows.stem: Which of the following d-orbitals experience more repulsion in the crystal field splitting of octahedral complex ?
rows.solution: In an octahedral complex the six ligands approach the metal straight along the \(x\), \(y\) and \(z\) axes. Two of the five d orbitals, \(d_{x^2-y^2}\) and \(d_{z^2}\), have their lobes pointing along exactly those axes, so an electron in either meets an incoming ligand lone pair head on and is repelled most strongly; these two rise in energy and form the \(e_g\) set. The other three, \(d_{xy}\), \(d_{yz}\) and \(d_{xz}\), point between the axes, further from the ligands, so they are repelled less and fall in energy to form the \(t_{2g}\) set.

rows.subtopic: Importance and Applications of Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: The chelating ligand used for the treatment of lead poisoning is :
rows.solution: EDTA, the ethylenediaminetetraacetate ion, is the chelating ligand used against lead poisoning. It is hexadentate, gripping a metal ion through four oxygen and two nitrogen donor atoms at once, and the resulting chelate is so stable and so water-soluble that the lead is locked up and excreted. Ethane-1,2-diamine and the oxalate ion are only bidentate and bind too weakly for the purpose; dimethylglyoxime is the reagent used to detect nickel.

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: Manganate ion is paramagnetic due to the presence of :
rows.solution: The manganate ion is \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{2-}}\). Each oxygen counts as \(-2\), so four of them give \(-8\), and for the ion to carry \(-2\) the manganese must be \(+6\). Manganese has 25 electrons, so \(\mathrm{Mn(VI)}\) is left with the configuration \(3d^1\) — one electron, and therefore one unpaired electron, which is what makes the green manganate ion paramagnetic. (For contrast, permanganate is \(\mathrm{Mn(VII)}\), \(3d^0\), and is diamagnetic; its intense purple comes from charge transfer, not from d electrons.)

rows.stem: The correct order of decreasing basicities of \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\) and \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_3N}\) in aqueous solution is :
rows.solution:
In water three influences act at once. The inductive effect of the ethyl groups raises basicity as more of them are added. Steric crowding lowers it, since bulky groups block a proton's approach. And solvation lowers it too: the more hydrogens the cation has on nitrogen, the more hydrogen bonds it can make to water and the better stabilised it is, so the primary amine's cation is best solvated and the tertiary amine's worst.

For ethyl groups the three effects settle out so that the secondary amine is the strongest base, the tertiary next and the primary last:
\((\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH} > (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_3\mathrm{N} > \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\)
This order is worth remembering as it stands, because for METHYL groups the answer is different — there the primary amine outranks the tertiary.

rows.stem: The boiling point of one molal NaCl solution, assuming NaCl to be completely dissociated in water is : (\(\mathrm{K_b}\) for water = \(0{\cdot}52\) K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\))
rows.solution:
Sodium chloride is completely dissociated, so each formula unit gives two ions and the van't Hoff factor is 2:
\(\Delta T_b = i\,K_b\,m = 2 \times 0.52 \times 1 = 1.04\ \mathrm{K}\)

Adding this to the boiling point of pure water,
\(T_b = 100 + 1.04 = 101.04\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\)

Forgetting the factor of 2 gives \(100.52\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\), which is one of the offered choices — the whole point of specifying that the salt is completely dissociated.

rows.stem: When a liquid and its vapour are at equilibrium and the pressure is suddenly decreased :

options.label: A
options.text: vapour pressure of the solution increases

rows.solution: At equilibrium the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation. Drop the pressure suddenly and condensation is no longer keeping pace, so the system responds by evaporating more liquid to restore the balance. Evaporation needs the latent heat of vaporisation, and with no heat supplied from outside it has to come from the liquid itself. The liquid therefore loses energy and its temperature falls: cooling occurs. This is the principle a refrigerant works on.

rows.stem:
Consider the following cell at 298 K :
\(\mathrm{Mg\,(s)\,|\,Mg^{2+}\,(1{\cdot}0\ M)\,||\,Cu^{2+}\,(1{\cdot}0\ M)\,|\,Cu\,(s)}\)
How can we increase the emf of the cell using the same substances ?

options.label: A
options.text: By decreasing only the \(\mathrm{[Mg^{2+}]}\) to \(0{\cdot}1\) M

options.label: B
options.text: By decreasing only the \(\mathrm{[Cu^{2+}]}\) to \(0{\cdot}1\) M

options.label: C
options.text: By increasing both \(\mathrm{[Mg^{2+}]}\) and \(\mathrm{[Cu^{2+}]}\) to \(2{\cdot}0\) M

options.label: D
options.text: By increasing only the \(\mathrm{[Mg^{2+}]}\) to \(2{\cdot}0\) M

rows.solution:
For this cell the Nernst equation reads
\(E_{cell} = E^{\circ}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]}\)

The emf rises when the logarithm falls, that is when the ratio \([\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}]/[\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}]\) is made smaller. Lowering the magnesium ion concentration to 0.1 M does exactly that: the ratio becomes 0.1, its logarithm is negative, and the emf increases. Lowering the copper ion concentration instead would raise the ratio and lower the emf; raising the magnesium ion concentration would do the same; and multiplying both by the same factor leaves the ratio, and hence the emf, unchanged.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The rate of a first order reaction is \(5{\cdot}6 \times 10^{-4}\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), when the concentration of reactant is \(0{\cdot}2\) mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\). The rate constant ‘k’ is :
rows.solution:
For a first order reaction the rate law is rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]\), so
\(k = \dfrac{\text{rate}}{[\mathrm{A}]} = \dfrac{5.6 \times 10^{-4}}{0.2} = 2.8 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\)

The units check the answer: dividing mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}\ s^{-1}}\) by mol \(\mathrm{L^{-1}}\) leaves \(\mathrm{s^{-1}}\), which is what a first order rate constant must carry.

rows.stem: Nucleic acids are polymers of :
rows.solution: A nucleic acid is a polynucleotide: its repeating unit is the nucleotide, which is a nitrogenous base joined to a pentose sugar and then to a phosphate group. The nucleoside is only part of that unit — base plus sugar, without the phosphate — and it is the phosphate that forms the backbone linkages between one unit and the next, so the polymer cannot be described as one of nucleosides. Amino acids are the units of proteins, and a pentose sugar is one component of a nucleotide rather than the whole of it.

rows.stem: In the reaction of NaOBr with amide, the carbonyl carbon is lost as :
rows.solution:
Sodium hypobromite brings about the Hofmann bromamide degradation, which converts an amide to a primary amine with one carbon fewer. That missing carbon is the carbonyl carbon, and the reaction is carried out in alkaline medium, so it leaves as the carbonate ion:
\(\mathrm{RCONH_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} + 4\mathrm{NaOH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{RNH_2} + \mathrm{Na_2CO_3} + 2\mathrm{NaBr} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Carbon dioxide could not survive in that alkali, and neither bicarbonate nor carbon monoxide is produced.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Alcohols act as Bronsted bases as well as Bronsted acids.
Reason (R) : It is due to the presence of unshared electron pairs on oxygen atom and presence of polar O – H bond.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: An alcohol has two features at the same oxygen. It carries unshared electron pairs, so it can accept a proton and act as a Bronsted base — which is exactly what happens in the first step of acid catalysed dehydration. It also has a polar \(\mathrm{O-H}\) bond, so it can donate that proton and act as a Bronsted acid, as it does in its reaction with sodium. Both statements are therefore true, and the Reason names precisely the two structural features responsible for the two behaviours, so it is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Diazonium salts of aromatic amines are more stable than those of aliphatic amines.
Reason (R) : Diazonium salts of aliphatic amines undergo resonance.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Aromatic diazonium salts really are far more stable than aliphatic ones, so much so that they can be isolated and stored at low temperature while the aliphatic ones decompose at once. So the Assertion is true.

The Reason has the chemistry the wrong way round. Stability comes from resonance: in an aryl diazonium salt the positive charge is delocalised over the benzene ring, which is why it survives. An aliphatic diazonium ion has no such delocalisation — it loses nitrogen immediately to give a carbocation. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : For complex reaction, order of reaction is given by the slowest step.
Reason (R) : Order of a reaction is an experimental quantity.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
For a complex reaction the observed rate is set by the slowest step, the rate-determining step, and the order is read from the rate law that step produces. So the Assertion is true. Order is also an experimentally determined quantity rather than something read off the balanced equation, so the Reason is true as well.

They are not cause and effect, though. Being experimentally determined is a statement about how order is MEASURED; that the slowest step fixes it is a statement about the MECHANISM. So both are true but the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Sc^{3+}/Sc^{2+}}}\) has low value.
Reason (R) : Because of the stability of \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) ion which has a noble gas configuration.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The electrode potential in question is for the reduction \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}} + e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{Sc^{2+}}\), and its value is very low, that is strongly negative. So the Assertion is true.

The reason is the stability of the ion being reduced. Scandium has the configuration \([\mathrm{Ar}]3d^1 4s^2\), so losing three electrons leaves \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) with the noble gas configuration of argon and no d electron at all. Such an ion has no tendency to accept an electron back, so the reduction is strongly disfavoured and the potential is low. Both statements are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
(a) Reactions of which order will show the rate to be independent of the concentration of the reactant ? Give one example of this order.
(b) State the condition under which a bimolecular reaction may be kinetically a first order reaction.
rows.solution:
(a) A zero order reaction. Its rate law is rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}]^0 = k\), so the rate is a constant and does not change as the reactant is used up. The standard example is the decomposition of gaseous ammonia on a hot platinum surface at high pressure; the decomposition of hydrogen iodide on a gold surface behaves the same way. In both cases the metal surface is already saturated with reactant, so adding more changes nothing.

(b) When one of the two reactants is present in large excess. Its concentration then barely changes as the reaction proceeds and can be absorbed into the rate constant, so rate \(= k[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}]\) becomes rate \(= k'[\mathrm{A}]\). The reaction is still bimolecular in mechanism but behaves as first order in kinetics, which is why it is called a pseudo first order reaction. The acid hydrolysis of an ester in dilute aqueous solution is the usual example, water being the reactant in excess.

rows.stem:
Explain the following with the help of Henry’s law :
(i) Bends
(ii) Anoxia
rows.solution:
Henry's law says that the mass of a gas dissolving in a given volume of liquid at constant temperature is proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid. Both conditions follow from that single sentence, read in opposite directions.

(i) Bends. A scuba diver breathes compressed air, so at depth the partial pressures are high and more nitrogen dissolves in the blood than at the surface. If the diver comes up quickly the pressure falls sharply, the blood is suddenly supersaturated, and the excess nitrogen comes out of solution as bubbles inside the capillaries and blocks them. The result is the painful and dangerous condition called bends. Divers therefore ascend slowly, and their tanks are filled with air diluted by helium, which is much less soluble.

(ii) Anoxia. At high altitude the atmospheric pressure is low, so the partial pressure of oxygen is low, and by Henry's law less oxygen dissolves in the blood. Tissues are starved of oxygen, and the climber becomes weak and unable to think clearly. This condition is called anoxia.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: How does sprinkling of salt help in clearing the snow covered roads in hilly areas ? Write the name of the colligative property involved in this process.
rows.solution:
Sprinkling salt on snow lowers the freezing point of the water. Salt dissolves in the thin film of liquid water always present on the snow, and a solution freezes below \(0\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\); the ice is then above its own freezing point and melts, and more salt dissolves in the melt so the process continues. The snow turns to a solution that runs off, and the road clears.

The colligative property involved is depression of freezing point.

rows.stem:
Write IUPAC names of the following compounds :
(a) \(\mathrm{[Cr(NH_3)_4\,(ONO)Cl]\,NO_3}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{Na[Ag(CN)_2]}\)
rows.solution:
(a) The nitrate ion outside carries \(-1\), so the complex cation is \(+1\). Inside it, the chlorido ligand is \(-1\), the nitrito ligand is \(-1\), and the four ammine ligands are neutral, so chromium must be \(+3\). The ligands are cited alphabetically — ammine, chlorido, then nitrito — and \(\mathrm{ONO}\) means the ligand is attached through its oxygen, which is shown as nitrito-O. The name is tetraamminechloridonitrito-O-chromium(III) nitrate.

(b) The sodium ion contributes \(+1\), so the complex anion is \(-1\). Two cyanido ligands contribute \(-2\), which leaves silver at \(+1\). An anionic complex takes the Latin stem of the metal with the \(-ate\) ending, so silver becomes argentate. The name is sodium dicyanidoargentate(I).

rows.stem:
What are the hydrolysis products of the following ?
(a) Lactose
(b) DNA containing Thymine
rows.solution:
(a) Lactose is a disaccharide of one glucose unit and one galactose unit joined by a \(\beta\)-1,4 glycosidic linkage, so hydrolysis gives D-(+)-glucose and D-(+)-galactose.

(b) A DNA nucleotide containing thymine hydrolyses into its three components: the base thymine, the sugar 2-deoxy-D-ribose, and phosphoric acid.

rows.stem:
Draw the structures of major product(s) in each of the following reactions :
(a) 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{(ii)\ H^{+}}]{\mathrm{(i)\ NaOH,\ 368\ K}}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{CH_3CH = C(CH_3)_2 + HBr \longrightarrow}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — part (a)'s substrate is printed as a SKELETAL DRAWING: a benzene ring carrying Cl at C1, \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) at C2 and \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) at C4 (positions confirmed at 4x). It is NAMED losslessly in the stem as 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrobenzene, so the row is answerable from text alone; naming a reactant cannot state the answer here because the question asks for the PRODUCT. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) Chlorine on a benzene ring is normally inert to nucleophiles, but two nitro groups ortho and para to it change that completely: they withdraw electron density and, more importantly, stabilise by resonance the negative charge of the intermediate formed when hydroxide attacks. Substitution therefore proceeds under moderate conditions, and acidification of the phenoxide gives the phenol. The product is 2,4-dinitrophenol — a benzene ring carrying \(-\mathrm{OH}\) at position 1 and \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) at positions 2 and 4.

(b) Addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) to an unsymmetrical alkene follows Markovnikov's rule, the hydrogen going to the carbon that already carries more hydrogens so that the more stable carbocation forms. In \(\mathrm{CH_3CH{=}C(CH_3)_2}\) the left-hand alkene carbon has one hydrogen and the right-hand one has none, so the proton adds on the left and the bromide is captured by the resulting tertiary cation on the right:
\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH{=}C(CH_3)_2} + \mathrm{HBr} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CBr(CH_3)-CH_3}\)
The major product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane.

rows.stem:
Write the structures of A, B and C in the following reactions :
(a) Aniline \(\xrightarrow[\mathrm{CH_3COOH}]{\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}}\) A \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}}\) B \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^{+}}}\) C
(b) 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Fe + HCl}}\) A \(\xrightarrow[273 - 278\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HCl}}\) B \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_3PO_2 + H_2O}}\) C
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — both substrates are printed as SKELETAL DRAWINGS: (a) a benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{NH_2}\), and (b) a benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) at C1, Br at C2 and \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) at C4 (positions confirmed at 4x). Both are NAMED losslessly in the stem (aniline; 2-bromo-4-nitrotoluene), so the row is answerable from text; the question asks for the products A, B and C, so naming the reactants cannot state the answer. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) Acetic anhydride acetylates the amino group, giving acetanilide:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5-NHCOCH_3}\)
The point of acetylating first is control: \(-\mathrm{NHCOCH_3}\) is still ortho, para directing but much less strongly activating than \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\), so bromination stops cleanly at one substitution, and the bulk of the group sends it para.
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{4\text{-}Br{-}C_6H_4{-}NHCOCH_3}\), p-bromoacetanilide
Acid hydrolysis then removes the acetyl group and returns the free amine:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{4\text{-}Br{-}C_6H_4{-}NH_2}\), p-bromoaniline

(b) Iron with hydrochloric acid reduces the nitro group to an amino group and leaves the bromine and the methyl group alone:
\(\mathrm{A} = \) 2-bromo-4-methylaniline, the ring carrying \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\), with \(-\mathrm{Br}\) ortho to it and \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) para to it.
Sodium nitrite in hydrochloric acid at \(273-278\ \mathrm{K}\) diazotises that amine:
\(\mathrm{B} = \) the corresponding benzenediazonium chloride, \(\mathrm{-N_2^+Cl^-}\) in place of \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\).
Hypophosphorous acid with water then replaces the diazonium group by hydrogen, removing the nitrogen as gas:
\(\mathrm{C} = \) 2-bromotoluene.
The sequence is the standard way of REMOVING an amino group from a ring after it has done its directing work.

rows.stem:
What happens when :
(a) Propanenitrile is treated with phenyl magnesium bromide followed by hydrolysis ?
(b) p-fluorotoluene is treated with \(\mathrm{CrO_3}\) in the presence of acetic anhydride followed by hydrolysis with aqueous acid.
(c) Phthalic acid is treated with \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) followed by heating ?
Write chemical reactions in support of your answer.
rows.solution:
(a) A Grignard reagent adds across the carbon-nitrogen triple bond of a nitrile, and hydrolysis of the adduct gives a ketone. The nitrile carbon becomes the carbonyl carbon:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CN} + \mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]{\text{dry ether}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CO-CH_2CH_3}\)
The product is 1-phenylpropan-1-one.

(b) Chromium trioxide in acetic anhydride oxidises the methyl group on the ring, but the anhydride converts the aldehyde as it forms into a gem-diacetate, which protects it from further oxidation. Hydrolysis with aqueous acid then releases the aldehyde:
\(\mathrm{4\text{-}F{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) }\mathrm{H_3O^+}]{\text{(i) }\mathrm{CrO_3}/(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{4\text{-}F{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO}\)
The product is 4-fluorobenzaldehyde.

(c) Ammonia first converts both carboxyl groups into ammonium salts, and heating then drives off water from each to leave the diamide:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_4(COOH)_2} + 2\mathrm{NH_3} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C_6H_4(COONH_4)_2} \xrightarrow[-2\mathrm{H_2O}]{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_4(CONH_2)_2}\)
The product is benzene-1,2-dicarboxamide, phthalamide. Continued strong heating takes it one step further, expelling ammonia and closing the five-membered ring to give phthalimide.

rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :
(a) Why is direct current (DC) not used to measure the resistance of an ionic solution ?
(b) Why are the products of electrolysis different for the electrolysis of aqueous solution of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) with silver electrodes and electrolysis of aqueous solution of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) with platinum electrodes ?
(c) Why are magnesium blocks fixed to the iron pipelines carrying water ?
rows.solution:
(a) Direct current would electrolyse the solution. A steady current in one direction discharges ions at the electrodes, so the composition of the solution changes while the measurement is being made, and the products that collect on the electrodes polarise them and add an unknown resistance of their own. Alternating current avoids both problems: it reverses many times a second, so no net electrolysis occurs and nothing accumulates.

(b) The cathode behaves the same way in both cases — silver ions are reduced and silver is deposited. The anode is where they differ. Silver is a reactive electrode, so instead of any solution species being oxidised the electrode itself dissolves: \(\mathrm{Ag(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ag^+(aq)} + e^-\). Platinum is inert and takes no part in the chemistry; it only carries electrons away, so water is oxidised instead and oxygen gas is released. This is exactly why electroplating uses an electrode of the plating metal.

(c) This is cathodic protection. Magnesium has a far more negative electrode potential than iron, so when the two are in contact the magnesium is oxidised in preference and the iron is not. The magnesium block corrodes away as a sacrificial anode, keeping the pipeline intact, and is replaced periodically.

rows.stem: When a coordination compound \(\mathrm{CoCl_3 \cdot 6NH_3}\) is mixed with excess of \(\mathrm{AgNO_3}\) solution, 3 moles of AgCl are precipitated per mole of the compound. Write the structural formula of the complex, IUPAC name, its hybridisation and magnetic behaviour on the basis of valence bond theory.
rows.solution:
Three moles of silver chloride per mole of compound means all three chloride ions are free in solution, so none of them is inside the coordination sphere. All six ammonia molecules must therefore be the ligands, and the three chlorides are counter ions.

Structural formula: \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3}\)

IUPAC name: hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride

Cobalt is \(+3\), so \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\). Ammonia is a strong field ligand, so it forces the six d electrons to pair into three of the \(3d\) orbitals, leaving two \(3d\) orbitals empty. Those two, with the \(4s\) and three \(4p\) orbitals, give the hybridisation:

Hybridisation: \(d^2sp^3\), an inner orbital octahedral complex.

Magnetic behaviour: with every electron paired, the complex is diamagnetic.

rows.stem:
(i) How many geometrical isomers are possible in each of the following complexes ?
(I) \(\mathrm{[Cr(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\)
(II) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3Cl_3]}\)
(ii) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) is an inner orbital complex whereas \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]^{2+}}\) is an outer orbital complex. Why ?
[Atomic number : Co = 27, Ni = 28]
(iii) Write the formula of Wilkinson catalyst and its use.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) \(\mathrm{[Cr(C_2O_4)_3]^{3-}}\) has no geometrical isomers — zero. Three identical bidentate ligands on one metal can be arranged in only one way. The complex is not without isomerism, though: it has no plane of symmetry, so it exists as a pair of optical isomers.

(II) \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_3Cl_3]}\) has two geometrical isomers. In the facial isomer the three ammine ligands occupy one triangular face of the octahedron and the three chlorides the opposite one; in the meridional isomer each set of three lies along a meridian.

(ii) Both metal ions meet strong enough ligands, but only one of them has room. Cobalt is \(+3\), so \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) is \(3d^6\); ammonia pairs those six electrons into three orbitals and leaves TWO \(3d\) orbitals empty, which is exactly what \(d^2sp^3\) hybridisation needs — hence an inner orbital complex. Nickel is \(+2\), so \(\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}\) is \(3d^8\); even after pairing, eight electrons fill four orbitals and leave only ONE \(3d\) orbital free, and one is not enough. The bonding must then use outer \(4d\) orbitals, giving \(sp^3d^2\) and an outer orbital complex.

(iii) Wilkinson's catalyst is \(\mathrm{[(Ph_3P)_3RhCl]}\), chlorotris(triphenylphosphine)rhodium(I). It is used for the homogeneous hydrogenation of alkenes.

rows.stem: Calculate the vapour pressure of a solution containing 61 g of benzoic acid (molar mass = 122 g \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)) dissolved in 500 g of benzene when the vapour pressure of pure benzene at this temperature of experiment is 66 torr. Assume complete dimerization of benzoic acid in benzene.
rows.solution:
Benzoic acid dimerises completely in benzene, so two molecules give one particle and the van't Hoff factor is \(i = 0.5\).

Relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of the solute, corrected by \(i\):
\(\dfrac{p_1^{\circ} - p_1}{p_1^{\circ}} = i\,x_2\)

For a dilute solution \(x_2\) may be taken as \(n_2/n_1\), which gives
\(\dfrac{66 - p_1}{66} = 0.5 \times \dfrac{61 \times 78}{122 \times 500} = 0.5 \times 0.078 = 0.039\)
\(66 - p_1 = 66 \times 0.039 = 2.574\)
\(p_1 = 63.4\ \mathrm{torr}\)

Working without that approximation, with \(n_2 = \dfrac{61}{122} = 0.5\) and \(n_1 = \dfrac{500}{78} = 6.41\),
\(\dfrac{66 - p_1}{66} = 0.5 \times \dfrac{0.5}{6.41 + 0.5} = 0.5 \times 0.0724 = 0.0362\)
\(p_1 = 63.61\ \mathrm{torr}\)

Both are accepted. The two differ by about \(0.2\) torr, which is the whole cost of the dilute-solution approximation here.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Consider the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide \(\mathrm{(H_2O_2)}\) as per the equation given below :
\(\mathrm{2H_2O_2} \xrightarrow[\text{Alkaline medium}]{\mathrm{I^{-}}} \mathrm{2H_2O + O_2}\)
The mechanism for this reaction was found to be :
Step I : \(\mathrm{H_2O_2 + I^{-} \longrightarrow H_2O + IO^{-}}\) (slow)
Step II : \(\mathrm{H_2O_2 + IO^{-} \longrightarrow H_2O + I^{-} + O_2}\) (fast)
(a) Write the rate law expression.
(b) Determine the order of reaction with respect to \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\), \(\mathrm{I^{-}}\) and overall order of reaction.
(c) What is the molecularity of the reaction in Step II ?
rows.solution:
(a) The rate of a multi-step reaction is set by its slowest step, and only the species present in that step appear in the rate law. Step I consumes one \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) and one \(\mathrm{I^-}\), so
\(\text{Rate} = k[\mathrm{H_2O_2}][\mathrm{I^-}]\)

(b) Reading the exponents straight off that expression: the order with respect to \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) is 1, the order with respect to \(\mathrm{I^-}\) is 1, and the overall order is \(1 + 1 = 2\).

Note that the iodide ion does not appear in the balanced overall equation at all — it is regenerated in Step II and acts as a catalyst — yet it appears in the rate law. That is precisely why order must be measured rather than read off the equation.

(c) Step II involves a collision between one \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) molecule and one \(\mathrm{IO^-}\) ion, so its molecularity is 2.

rows.stem:
Answer the following :
(a) Which isomer of \(\mathrm{C_4H_9Br}\) is most reactive towards \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction ?
(b) Predict the alkene that would be formed by dehydrohalogenation of 1-Bromo-1-methylcyclohexane.
(c) Although chlorine shows strong – I effect, yet it is ortho- and para-directing in electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions. Why ?
rows.solution:
(a) An \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction proceeds through a carbocation, so the fastest isomer is the one giving the most stable cation. That is the tertiary halide, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{CBr}\), whose cation is stabilised by three alkyl groups.

(b) Dehydrohalogenation removes the bromine together with a hydrogen from an adjacent carbon. In 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane the bromine sits on a ring carbon that also carries a methyl group, so the hydrogen may come either from a neighbouring ring carbon or from the methyl group. Removing a ring hydrogen gives the more substituted, and therefore more stable, alkene, and by Saytzeff's rule that is the major product: 1-methylcyclohexene, the double bond inside the ring. The minor product, from the methyl group, is methylenecyclohexane.

(c) The two effects of chlorine answer two different questions. Its \(-I\) effect withdraws electron density from the whole ring, which slows every electrophilic substitution down: chlorobenzene reacts more slowly than benzene, so chlorine is deactivating. But chlorine also has lone pairs, and its \(+R\) effect donates one into the ring, concentrating electron density at the ortho and para positions. When an electrophile attacks there, the carbocation intermediate gains an extra resonance structure in which chlorine bears the positive charge; no such structure is available for meta attack. So the RATE is set by \(-I\) and the POSITION by \(+R\), and chlorine is deactivating and ortho, para directing at the same time.

rows.stem: Write the mechanism of acid dehydration of ethanol to yield ethene.
rows.context: Alcohols and Phenols are acidic in nature. Electron withdrawing groups in phenol increase its acidic strength and electron releasing groups decrease it. Alcohols undergo nucleophilic substitution with hydrogen halides to yield alkyl halides. Dehydration of alcohols gives alkenes. On oxidation, primary alcohols yield aldehydes with mild oxidising agents and carboxylic acids with strong oxidising agents, while secondary alcohols yield ketones. Tertiary alcohols are resistant to oxidation. The presence of – OH group in phenols activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions due to resonance effect.
rows.solution:
Acid catalysed dehydration of ethanol to ethene runs in three steps.

Step 1 — protonation of the alcohol. The oxygen uses one of its lone pairs to pick up a proton from the acid, giving the protonated alcohol, an oxonium ion. This step is fast and reversible.
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-OH} + \mathrm{H^+} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2}\)

Step 2 — formation of the carbocation. The protonated alcohol loses a molecule of water. This is the slow, rate-determining step, because a bond breaks and a charged species is created; what remains is the ethyl carbocation.
\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2-\overset{+}{O}H_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_3-\overset{+}{C}H_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Step 3 — deprotonation. A base, usually a water molecule, removes a proton from the carbon next to the positive centre, and the pair of electrons left behind forms the double bond. The catalyst is returned.
\(\mathrm{CH_3-\overset{+}{C}H_2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH_2{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{H^+}\)

rows.stem: Why are tertiary alcohols resistant to oxidation ?
rows.context: Alcohols and Phenols are acidic in nature. Electron withdrawing groups in phenol increase its acidic strength and electron releasing groups decrease it. Alcohols undergo nucleophilic substitution with hydrogen halides to yield alkyl halides. Dehydration of alcohols gives alkenes. On oxidation, primary alcohols yield aldehydes with mild oxidising agents and carboxylic acids with strong oxidising agents, while secondary alcohols yield ketones. Tertiary alcohols are resistant to oxidation. The presence of – OH group in phenols activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions due to resonance effect.
rows.solution: Oxidising an alcohol means removing the hydrogen from the carbon that bears the \(-\mathrm{OH}\), together with the hydrogen of the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) itself, and forming a carbon-oxygen double bond in their place. A tertiary alcohol has no hydrogen at all on that carbon, since all three of its remaining valencies are taken by alkyl groups, so the double bond cannot form and the alcohol resists oxidation. Under very drastic conditions it can be attacked, but only by breaking carbon-carbon bonds, which gives a mixture of smaller fragments rather than a single clean product.

rows.stem: Write the structure of the major product expected from the dinitration of 3-methylphenol.
rows.context: Alcohols and Phenols are acidic in nature. Electron withdrawing groups in phenol increase its acidic strength and electron releasing groups decrease it. Alcohols undergo nucleophilic substitution with hydrogen halides to yield alkyl halides. Dehydration of alcohols gives alkenes. On oxidation, primary alcohols yield aldehydes with mild oxidising agents and carboxylic acids with strong oxidising agents, while secondary alcohols yield ketones. Tertiary alcohols are resistant to oxidation. The presence of – OH group in phenols activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions due to resonance effect.
rows.solution:
In 3-methylphenol both substituents are activating and both are ortho, para directing, and — this is what makes the answer clean — they agree with each other. Taking the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) carbon as position 1 and the \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) as position 3, the positions ortho and para to the hydroxyl group are 2, 6 and 4, while those ortho and para to the methyl group are 2, 4 and 6. Position 2 lies between the two substituents and is too crowded, so the two nitro groups enter at 4 and 6.

The major product is 3-methyl-4,6-dinitrophenol: a benzene ring carrying \(-\mathrm{OH}\) at position 1, \(-\mathrm{CH_3}\) at position 3, and \(-\mathrm{NO_2}\) at positions 4 and 6.

rows.stem: Why is ortho-nitrophenol more acidic than ortho-methoxyphenol ?
rows.context: Alcohols and Phenols are acidic in nature. Electron withdrawing groups in phenol increase its acidic strength and electron releasing groups decrease it. Alcohols undergo nucleophilic substitution with hydrogen halides to yield alkyl halides. Dehydration of alcohols gives alkenes. On oxidation, primary alcohols yield aldehydes with mild oxidising agents and carboxylic acids with strong oxidising agents, while secondary alcohols yield ketones. Tertiary alcohols are resistant to oxidation. The presence of – OH group in phenols activates the aromatic ring towards electrophilic substitution and directs the incoming group to ortho and para positions due to resonance effect.
rows.solution: Acidity is decided by how stable the phenoxide ion is once the proton has gone. The nitro group withdraws electron density both inductively and by resonance, and in the ortho position it can accept the negative charge onto its own oxygen atoms, so the phenoxide from ortho-nitrophenol is well stabilised and the proton leaves readily. The methoxy group does the opposite: its oxygen donates a lone pair into the ring by resonance, pushing electron density towards the negative charge and destabilising the phenoxide, so that proton is harder to remove. Ortho-nitrophenol is therefore the more acidic of the two.

rows.stem:
How do you explain the following ?
(i) Presence of a carbonyl group in glucose
(ii) Presence of five – OH groups in glucose which are attached to different carbon atoms.
rows.context:
Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or the compounds which produce such units on hydrolysis. They have been broadly classified into three groups — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. The carbohydrates may also be classified as either reducing or non-reducing sugars. An important monosaccharide glucose is an aldohexose and is correctly named as D(+)–glucose. It was assigned the open structure on the basis of its reactions with HI, \(\mathrm{NH_2OH}\), \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water, \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\) and nitric acid.
Despite having the – CHO group, glucose does not give Schiff’s test and hydrogen sulphite addition product with \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\). It was found that glucose forms a six-membered ring in which one of the – OH groups add to the – CHO group and form a cyclic hemiacetal structure.
rows.solution:
(i) Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine to give an oxime, and with hydrogen cyanide to give a cyanohydrin:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_2N-OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH{=}N-OH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
Both are addition reactions characteristic of a carbonyl group, so a carbonyl group must be present. That it is an aldehyde rather than a ketone follows from glucose reducing Tollens' reagent.

(ii) Glucose reacts with acetic anhydride to give a stable pentaacetate, that is a derivative carrying exactly five acetyl groups. Acetylation occurs at hydroxyl groups, so there are five of them. That they sit on five DIFFERENT carbons follows from the compound being stable: two hydroxyl groups on one carbon would make a gem-diol, which loses water immediately.

rows.stem: What type of carbohydrates are called reducing sugars ?
rows.context:
Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or the compounds which produce such units on hydrolysis. They have been broadly classified into three groups — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. The carbohydrates may also be classified as either reducing or non-reducing sugars. An important monosaccharide glucose is an aldohexose and is correctly named as D(+)–glucose. It was assigned the open structure on the basis of its reactions with HI, \(\mathrm{NH_2OH}\), \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water, \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\) and nitric acid.
Despite having the – CHO group, glucose does not give Schiff’s test and hydrogen sulphite addition product with \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\). It was found that glucose forms a six-membered ring in which one of the – OH groups add to the – CHO group and form a cyclic hemiacetal structure.
rows.solution: A reducing sugar is a carbohydrate that reduces Fehling's solution or Tollens' reagent. All monosaccharides, whether aldoses or ketoses, are reducing sugars, and so are those disaccharides in which a free aldehydic or ketonic group remains — maltose and lactose. Sucrose is not, because the linkage in it ties up the reducing groups of both its units.

rows.stem: In D(+)–glucose, what do the letter ‘D’ and sign ‘(+)’ represent ?
rows.context:
Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or the compounds which produce such units on hydrolysis. They have been broadly classified into three groups — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. The carbohydrates may also be classified as either reducing or non-reducing sugars. An important monosaccharide glucose is an aldohexose and is correctly named as D(+)–glucose. It was assigned the open structure on the basis of its reactions with HI, \(\mathrm{NH_2OH}\), \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water, \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\) and nitric acid.
Despite having the – CHO group, glucose does not give Schiff’s test and hydrogen sulphite addition product with \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\). It was found that glucose forms a six-membered ring in which one of the – OH groups add to the – CHO group and form a cyclic hemiacetal structure.
rows.solution:
The two symbols carry quite different information, which is the point of the question.

The capital \(\mathrm{D}\) describes CONFIGURATION: it says that the \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group on the chiral carbon farthest from the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) group lies on the right in the Fischer projection, the same arrangement as in (+)-glyceraldehyde, which is the reference compound.

The sign \((+)\) describes OPTICAL ROTATION as measured: it says the compound is dextrorotatory, rotating the plane of polarised light to the right. It is determined by experiment and cannot be predicted from the configuration, which is why both symbols are needed.

rows.stem: Draw the six-membered ring structure of \(\alpha\)–D(+)–glucose.
rows.context:
Carbohydrates are optically active polyhydroxy aldehydes or ketones or the compounds which produce such units on hydrolysis. They have been broadly classified into three groups — monosaccharides, oligosaccharides and polysaccharides. The carbohydrates may also be classified as either reducing or non-reducing sugars. An important monosaccharide glucose is an aldohexose and is correctly named as D(+)–glucose. It was assigned the open structure on the basis of its reactions with HI, \(\mathrm{NH_2OH}\), \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) water, \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\) and nitric acid.
Despite having the – CHO group, glucose does not give Schiff’s test and hydrogen sulphite addition product with \(\mathrm{NaHSO_3}\). It was found that glucose forms a six-membered ring in which one of the – OH groups add to the – CHO group and form a cyclic hemiacetal structure.
rows.solution:
The six-membered ring form of \(\alpha\)-D-(+)-glucose is the pyranose ring, drawn as a Haworth projection: a flat hexagon seen edge-on, with the ring oxygen at the back right and the carbons numbered clockwise from the anomeric carbon, C-1, at the right.

Going round the ring: C-1 carries \(-\mathrm{OH}\) pointing DOWN and \(-\mathrm{H}\) up; C-2 carries \(-\mathrm{OH}\) down and \(-\mathrm{H}\) up; C-3 carries \(-\mathrm{OH}\) up and \(-\mathrm{H}\) down; C-4 carries \(-\mathrm{OH}\) down and \(-\mathrm{H}\) up; C-5 carries \(-\mathrm{H}\) down and the \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) group, which is C-6, pointing UP; and the ring oxygen bridges C-5 to C-1.

What makes it the \(\alpha\) anomer is the C-1 hydroxyl pointing DOWN, on the side opposite the \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\) group. In \(\beta\)-D-glucose that one hydroxyl points up instead, and nothing else changes.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
(i) Account for the following :
(I) MnO is basic while \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}\) is acidic.
(II) Iron has higher enthalpy of atomization than that of copper.
(III) \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is a stronger oxidising agent than \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\).
(ii) How do you prepare potassium dichromate from sodium chromate ? Write balanced chemical equation for each step.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) Both are oxides of manganese, and the oxidation state decides the character. In MnO manganese is \(+2\), a low oxidation state in which the metal keeps its metallic, electropositive character, so the oxide is ionic and basic. In \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}\) manganese is \(+7\); at that charge the metal pulls electron density strongly towards itself, the bonding becomes covalent, and the oxide behaves as an acid, dissolving in water to give permanganic acid. Rising oxidation state takes a transition metal oxide from basic through amphoteric to acidic.

(II) Enthalpy of atomisation measures how much energy is needed to pull the metal apart into free atoms, so it measures the strength of the metallic bonding — which depends on the number of unpaired electrons each atom contributes. Iron is \(3d^6 4s^2\) with four unpaired d electrons available; copper is \(3d^{10} 4s^1\), its d subshell completely filled and paired, leaving only the \(4s\) electron. Iron's bonding is therefore much the stronger and its enthalpy of atomisation the higher.

(III) A strong oxidising agent is one that is readily reduced. \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\), \(3d^4\), gains a great deal by accepting an electron, because doing so gives \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), \(3d^5\), a half-filled subshell of special stability. \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\), by contrast, is \(3d^3\) with a half-filled \(t_{2g}\) set and is already in a stable configuration, so it has little tendency to be reduced to \(\mathrm{Cr^{2+}}\). Hence \(\mathrm{Mn^{3+}}\) is the stronger oxidising agent.

(ii) Two steps. Acidify the sodium chromate solution, which converts the yellow chromate to the orange dichromate:
\(2\mathrm{Na_2CrO_4} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{Na^+} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
Then treat the sodium dichromate with potassium chloride. Potassium dichromate is much the less soluble salt, so it crystallises out and drives the exchange:
\(\mathrm{Na_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{KCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7} + 2\mathrm{NaCl}\)

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Answer the following questions :
(i) Why is chemistry of actinoids more complicated as compared to lanthanoids ?
(ii) \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{M^{2+}/M}}\) values are not regular for first row transition elements (3d series). Why ?
(iii) Identify the following :
(I) Oxoanion of chromium which is stable in acidic medium.
(II) The lanthanoid element that exhibits +4 oxidation state.
(iv) Write the products obtained on heating \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\).
(v) Predict which of the following ions will be coloured in aqueous solution :
\(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\), \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\), \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\), \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\)
rows.solution:
(i) Two things complicate actinoid chemistry. They are all radioactive, so they are difficult and hazardous to handle and many of them exist only in tiny amounts, prepared artificially. And they show a much wider range of oxidation states than the lanthanoids, because their 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals lie so close in energy that comparable numbers of electrons can be lost from all three — uranium alone runs from \(+3\) to \(+6\), where the lanthanoids are overwhelmingly \(+3\).

(ii) Because \(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{M^{2+}/M}}\) is not a single quantity but the net result of three, and each of them varies irregularly across the series: the enthalpy of atomisation of the metal, the sum of the first and second ionisation enthalpies \((\Delta_i H_1 + \Delta_i H_2)\), and the hydration enthalpy of the \(\mathrm{M^{2+}}\) ion. An irregularity in any one shows up in the electrode potential, and they do not cancel out.

(iii)(I) The dichromate ion, \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}\), is the oxoanion of chromium stable in acidic medium; in alkali it converts to chromate.
(II) Cerium exhibits the \(+4\) oxidation state, \(\mathrm{Ce^{4+}}\) being favoured because it leaves the empty \(4f^0\) configuration.

(iv) Heating potassium permanganate decomposes it, the manganese disproportionating to the \(+6\) manganate and the \(+4\) dioxide while oxygen is evolved:
\(2\mathrm{KMnO_4} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{K_2MnO_4} + \mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{O_2}\)

(v) Colour in these ions comes from a d-d transition, which needs a partly filled d subshell. \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) is \(3d^6\) and \(\mathrm{Ti^{3+}}\) is \(3d^1\), so both are coloured. \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\), \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) is \(3d^0\) and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is \(3d^{10}\); with an empty or a completely filled d subshell no d-d transition is possible, so those three are colourless.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) How will you bring about the following conversions :
(I) Bromobenzene to 1-phenylethanol
(II) Benzene to m-nitroacetophenone
(ii) An organic compound with the molecular formula \(\mathrm{C_8H_8O}\) forms 2,4-DNP derivative, reduces Tollens’ reagent and undergoes Cannizzaro reaction. On vigorous oxidation with acidic or alkaline \(\mathrm{KMnO_4}\) it gives Benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid. Identify the compound and write the products when it undergoes Cannizzaro reaction.
(iii) Arrange the following compounds in increasing order of their acid strength :
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\), \(\mathrm{O_2N - CH_2 - COOH}\), \(\mathrm{CF_3 - COOH}\), \(\mathrm{HCOOH}\)
rows.solution:
(i)(I) Bromobenzene to 1-phenylethanol. Make the Grignard reagent, add ethanal, then hydrolyse. The Grignard carbon attacks the carbonyl and the product after workup is the secondary alcohol:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5Br} \xrightarrow[\text{dry ether}]{\mathrm{Mg}} \mathrm{C_6H_5MgBr} \xrightarrow[\text{(ii) }\mathrm{H_2O}]{\text{(i) }\mathrm{CH_3CHO}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-CH(OH)-CH_3}\)

(II) Benzene to m-nitroacetophenone. The order of the two steps is the entire question. Acylate FIRST, because the \(-\mathrm{COCH_3}\) group introduced is deactivating and meta directing, so the nitration that follows delivers the nitro group to the meta position:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_6} \xrightarrow[\text{anhyd. }\mathrm{AlCl_3}]{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3} \xrightarrow[\text{conc. }\mathrm{H_2SO_4}]{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{3\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}COCH_3}\)
Nitrating first would give nitrobenzene, which is far too deactivated to undergo Friedel-Crafts acylation at all.

(ii) Every clue points one way. A 2,4-DNP derivative means a carbonyl group; reducing Tollens' reagent means specifically an aldehyde; undergoing Cannizzaro's reaction means no \(\alpha\) hydrogen, so the carbon next to the \(-\mathrm{CHO}\) must be part of the ring. Vigorous oxidation to benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid shows a second, oxidisable substituent ortho to the first. With \(\mathrm{C_8H_8O}\) that substituent is a methyl group, so the compound is 2-methylbenzaldehyde.

Cannizzaro's reaction makes it disproportionate: one molecule is oxidised to the salt of the acid and another reduced to the alcohol.
\(2\ \mathrm{2\text{-}CH_3{-}C_6H_4{-}CHO} + \mathrm{NaOH\ (conc.)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{2\text{-}CH_3{-}C_6H_4{-}COONa} + \mathrm{2\text{-}CH_3{-}C_6H_4{-}CH_2OH}\)

(iii) Acid strength rises as the group attached withdraws more electron density and so stabilises the carboxylate ion left behind. Benzoic acid is the weakest, the phenyl ring being only mildly withdrawing; formic acid is stronger, having no electron-releasing alkyl group at all; the nitro group of nitroacetic acid withdraws strongly; and the three fluorines of trifluoroacetic acid withdraw most of all. The increasing order is
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH} < \mathrm{HCOOH} < \mathrm{O_2N-CH_2-COOH} < \mathrm{CF_3-COOH}\)

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem:
(i) Write the products formed when benzaldehyde reacts with the following reagents :
(I) 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine
(II) Acetophenone in the presence of dilute NaOH followed by heating
(ii) Give reasons for the following :
(I) Benzoic acid does not undergo Friedel-Crafts reaction.
(II) Carboxylic acids have higher boiling point than alcohols of comparable molecular mass.
(iii) Write simple chemical test to distinguish between propanal and propanone.
rows.solution:
(i)(I) 2,4-Dinitrophenylhydrazine condenses with the carbonyl group, water being eliminated, to give the orange-red 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH{=}N-NH-C_6H_3(NO_2)_2}\)

(II) Benzaldehyde has no \(\alpha\) hydrogen and acetophenone has one, so with dilute alkali they undergo a crossed aldol condensation in only one direction: the carbanion from acetophenone attacks the aldehyde, and heating dehydrates the product. The result is the \(\alpha,\beta\)-unsaturated ketone
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5-CH{=}CH-CO-C_6H_5}\), 1,3-diphenylprop-2-en-1-one.

(ii)(I) Friedel-Crafts reactions need anhydrous aluminium chloride, a Lewis acid. The carboxyl group of benzoic acid is itself a Lewis base and binds to the aluminium chloride, forming a salt. That ties up the catalyst, and the positively charged complex left on the ring is strongly deactivating — so the ring, already deactivated by \(-\mathrm{COOH}\), becomes quite unreactive towards the electrophile.

(II) Carboxylic acid molecules associate in pairs through two intermolecular hydrogen bonds, each donating its \(-\mathrm{OH}\) proton to the carbonyl oxygen of the other, so in the liquid they exist largely as cyclic dimers. Breaking two hydrogen bonds per pair costs more energy than breaking the single hydrogen bond between one alcohol molecule and the next, so the acid boils higher.

(iii) Use Tollens' reagent. Warmed with a freshly prepared ammoniacal silver nitrate solution, propanal is oxidised and deposits a bright silver mirror on the tube; propanone, a ketone, gives no reaction. The iodoform test would serve equally well but the other way round — propanone responds and propanal does not.

rows.stem:
(i) Calculate \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{cell}}\) for the following reaction which is at equilibrium :
\(\mathrm{Cu\,(s) + 2Ag^{+}\,(aq) \rightleftharpoons Cu^{2+}\,(aq) + 2Ag\,(s)}\)
Equilibrium constant \(\mathrm{(K_c)}\) for the cell is \(10^{15}\).
[Given : log 10 = 1]
(ii) Write anode, cathode and overall reaction of lead storage battery when it is in use.
(iii) How much electricity is required in coulombs for the oxidation of 1 mol of FeO to \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\) ?
rows.solution:
(i) At equilibrium the cell has no net driving force, so \(E_{cell} = 0\) and the Nernst equation collapses to a relation between the standard emf and the equilibrium constant:
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = \dfrac{0.059}{n}\log K_c\)

Two electrons are transferred in this reaction, so \(n = 2\) and \(K_c = 10^{15}\):
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = \dfrac{0.059}{2}\log 10^{15} = \dfrac{0.059}{2} \times 15 = 0.0295 \times 15\)
\(E^{\circ}_{cell} = 0.4425\ \mathrm{V}\)

(ii) A lead storage battery in use is discharging, so it works as a galvanic cell: lead is oxidised at the anode and lead dioxide reduced at the cathode, both giving insoluble lead sulphate.
Anode: \(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2e^-\)
Cathode: \(\mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)} + 4\mathrm{H^+(aq)} + 2e^- \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)
Overall: \(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{PbO_2(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\)
The acid is consumed as the battery discharges, which is why its state of charge can be judged from the density of the electrolyte.

(iii) Work out the change in oxidation state, not the formula weights. In FeO iron is \(+2\); in \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\) it is \(+3\). So each iron atom loses one electron, and 1 mol of FeO means 1 mol of electrons:
\(Q = 1 \times F = 96500\ \mathrm{C}\)

rows.stem:
(i) Conductivity of \(0{\cdot}0024\) M acetic acid is \(7{\cdot}2 \times 10^{-5}\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\). If \(\Lambda^{\circ}_{m}\) for acetic acid is \(390{\cdot}5\) S \(\mathrm{cm^{2}}\) \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\), then calculate the degree of dissociation \((\alpha)\) of acetic acid.
(ii) Calculate the cell potential for the following half cell reaction at \(25\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) :
\(\mathrm{Ag^{+}\,(aq) + 1\,e^{-} \longrightarrow Ag\,(s)}\)
Given that : \(\mathrm{[Ag^{+}]}\) = \(0{\cdot}01\) M and
\(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Ag^{+}/Ag}}\) = + \(0{\cdot}80\) V
[log 10 = 1]
(iii) Write the name of the electrolyte used in :
(I) Dry cell
(II) Fuel cell \(\mathrm{(H_2 - O_2)}\)
rows.solution:
(i) First convert the conductivity into molar conductivity at this concentration:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C} = \dfrac{7.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 1000}{0.0024} = 30\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The degree of dissociation is then the ratio of this to the limiting value:
\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda^{\circ}_m} = \dfrac{30}{390.5} = 0.0768\), about \(0.077\)

So fewer than eight molecules in a hundred are dissociated at this concentration, which is what makes acetic acid a weak acid.

(ii) For a single electrode the Nernst equation is written for the reduction as given, with solid silver at unit activity:
\(E_{\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}} = E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Ag^+/Ag}} - \dfrac{0.059}{1}\log\dfrac{1}{[\mathrm{Ag^+}]}\)
\(= 0.80 - 0.059\log\dfrac{1}{0.01} = 0.80 - 0.059\log 10^{2}\)
\(= 0.80 - 0.059 \times 2 = 0.80 - 0.118\)
\(= 0.682\ \mathrm{V}\)

Note \(n = 1\) here, since the half reaction as written transfers a single electron. Diluting the solution below 1 M has lowered the potential, as it should: less \(\mathrm{Ag^+}\) present makes the reduction less favourable.

(iii)(I) In a dry cell the electrolyte is a moist paste of ammonium chloride and zinc chloride.
(II) In a hydrogen-oxygen fuel cell the electrolyte is a concentrated aqueous solution of an alkali, sodium hydroxide or potassium hydroxide.
